news.title: Scans of 153 Million Driver's Licenses Are Being Sold Online
news.excerpt: Criminals are selling pictures of more than 153 million driver's licenses stolen from a company that checks IDs for car rentals and stores — the FBI is investigating. With your license picture, a stranger can open cards or loans in your name. Do this today: pull your free credit report at annualcreditreport.com and freeze your credit for free at Equifax, Experian, and TransUnion — it stops new accounts cold. Expect a second wave: scam emails and calls offering to "help" you with this breach. Hang up and delete.

news.title: Fake 'Are You Human?' Checks Are Running Hidden Commands on Computers
news.excerpt: Those little boxes websites use to check "Are you human?" — scammers are putting up fakes. They ask you to press the Windows key and R, paste a code, and press Enter "to verify." What really happens is a hidden command runs that can sneak a bad program in or open a doorway into your computer. Microsoft and the FTC are warning about this trick right now. A real human check never asks you to run anything. If you see that, close the tab.

news.title: Fake QR Codes on Parking Meters Are Stealing Card Numbers — FTC Warns
news.excerpt: The FTC is warning about fake QR codes — the square black-and-white patterns you scan to pay for parking. Scammers print their own codes and stick them over the real ones on parking meters. Scan the wrong one and it opens a fake payment page that steals your card number. Before you pay, check the code: if it looks like a sticker slapped over the real sign, don't scan it. Type the parking service's web address yourself, pay at the machine, and report fakes at ReportFraud.ftc.gov.

news.title: Fake Car-Dealership Websites Are Taking Deposits — FTC Warns
news.excerpt: The Federal Trade Commission is warning about scammers cloning real car-dealership websites. They copy the logo, car photos, and customer reviews, then take an upfront deposit for a vehicle that doesn't exist. Buyers show up at the lot and find no record of their order or money. Before paying: search the dealer's name plus the word "scam," and insist on seeing the car in person or having an independent inspector check it. Never send a deposit by wire transfer. Report fake dealer sites at ReportFraud.ftc.gov. (Source: FTC, Sept. 1, 2026)

news.title: FBI Warning: One Click Can Hand Scammers Your Email — No Password Needed
news.excerpt: The FBI put out a warning yesterday about a new trick: scammers send you a link that opens a real-looking Google or Microsoft screen asking, "Allow this app access?" One click hands them your email — your messages, your contacts, your password-reset emails — even though your password never changed, and even with two-step sign-in on. Change your password afterward and they still stay logged in. Fix in two minutes: open your email account settings and look for "connected apps" or "third-party access," then remove anything you don't recognize. Never approve an access request you didn't start. (Source: According to the FBI's official Internet Crime Complaint Center, September 1, 2026)

posts.title: That "unpaid SunPass toll" text is fake — delete it and check your real balance at sunpass.com
posts.summary: The real SunPass never demands payment over a text message, and Florida's Attorney General has shut down fake toll sites before. Don't tap the link — delete the message, then check what you actually owe by signing in at **sunpass.com** or calling 1-888-TOLL-FLA (1-888-865-5352). Report the message free at **reportfraud.ftc.gov**.
posts.truth: These texts work because they land on a day you actually drove to Gainesville or Orlando, and six dollars sounds believable. The crooks only need one panicked tap. Here's the honest rule: no toll agency in Florida will ever ask you to settle up by tapping a link in a text — real invoices come by mail and inside your account. Delete first, then check the real balance yourself. More than one customer has told me they paid a fake toll site before something felt off.

posts.title: 153 million driver's licenses were stolen — check your free credit report at annualcreditreport.com
posts.summary: News broke this week that an identity-theft service is selling scanned driver's licenses for more than 153 million Americans and Canadians — and the FBI is investigating the company that collected them. Pull your free credit report at **annualcreditreport.com** (it's free every week, no catch), and freeze your credit for free at **Equifax**, **Experian**, and **TransUnion** so nobody can open a card or loan in your name.
posts.truth: Most people don't realize a stolen driver's license isn't about somebody driving as you — it's about opening credit cards and loans in your name. And here's the part that surprises everyone: freezing your credit doesn't change your life one bit. Your existing cards still work, you still buy what you normally buy — you just unfreeze for a day when you apply for something new, and freeze it again. It's 15 minutes of work at each of the three bureaus, it's free, and it's the closest thing to a lock on your front door that exists.

posts.title: Windows 11's Smart App Control stops bad apps before they run — turn it on free in Windows Security
posts.summary: Windows 11's Smart App Control checks every program before it opens and blocks the ones that look untrusted — and it's free, built right into Windows. Most computers just have it sitting there, turned off. To switch it on, open the Windows Security app that came with your computer, go to App & browser control, and turn on Smart App Control. It's about one click and it's from Microsoft. If your computer doesn't show the option, that's normal on some machines — bring it by and I'll set up the next-best protection for you.
posts.truth: Most people don't realize the scariest moment isn't when a bad program is already running — it's the two seconds before, when the computer hasn't decided yet. I see this all the time: someone downloads a 'free PDF converter' or a 'driver updater' out of an ad, and it's junk from the first click. Smart App Control is Microsoft's bouncer at the door — it checks a program's reputation before letting it in and stops a lot of the junk before it ever touches your files. It's not magic, but it's one of the best free layers I know, and most people have it sitting there, turned off.

posts.title: The Windows 11 September update finally brings back the movable taskbar — put it back at the top in Settings, free from Microsoft
posts.summary: Microsoft's September update for Windows 11 is rolling out now, and it brings back the choice owners have asked for since 2021: you can move the taskbar back to the top of the screen or to either side. Check for the update at Settings → Windows Update, then open Settings → Personalization → Taskbar → Taskbar behaviors and pick where you want it. It's free, built into Windows, and takes about a minute once the update is installed.
posts.truth: I've heard this since Windows 11 came out: 'John, can you move that bar back to the top? It's been up there for twenty years.' For a long time the honest answer was no — Microsoft took that choice away. Now it's back the normal way, in an update, no tricks or workarounds. Open Settings → Personalization → Taskbar once yours arrives — and don't let anybody charge you to 'fix' it.

posts.title: Google's free Security Checkup shows every device signed into your Gmail — run it in 2 minutes at myaccount.google.com/security-checkup
posts.summary: Run Google's free Security Checkup at myaccount.google.com/security-checkup. It lists every device signed into your Gmail and lets you sign out any device you don't recognize — it takes 2 minutes and Google walks you through it step by step.
posts.truth: Whoever gets into your email can reset your bank password, your Facebook, your Amazon — every "forgot password" email lands there. I see it all the time: a Gmail quietly still signed in on a computer sold at a yard sale two years ago. Looking at the device list is like checking who has a copy of your house key — you'd want to know.

posts.title: Windows 10 computers no longer get free security updates — check Windows Update for your free Windows 11 offer
posts.summary: On a Windows 10 PC, click **Start > Settings > Update & Security > Windows Update** and choose **Check for updates**. If your PC can run Windows 11, Microsoft's free offer appears right there — no purchase, no new computer, and your files stay put. If you see an offer for "Extended Security Updates" instead, that's Microsoft's safety net for older PCs — and it doesn't last forever.
posts.truth: Most people don't realize what "no more updates" really means: your banks, your email, and your protection programs all lean on that update stream, and an unpatched Windows 10 computer will still turn on and "work fine" right up until it doesn't. The honest answer is that plenty of these machines can make the free jump to Windows 11 today — but nobody gets told unless they look.

posts.title: Firefox's new update shows how many trackers it blocked right in the address bar — free at firefox.com
posts.summary: **Firefox**'s latest version, out September 1, puts a counter right in the address bar that shows how many ad trackers it stopped, and it loads pages faster with new AI help features on top. If you already use Firefox, it updates itself automatically — or download it free at **firefox.com**. Takes 2 minutes.
posts.truth: Most people don't realize your browser does two jobs at once: it shows you the page, and it quietly tells advertisers who you are and where you've been. Firefox blocks that second job by default now, and it shows you the count so you can see it working. The honest answer to "is my computer safe?" is: safer than it was last week — if you let your browser update itself.

posts.title: That slow old laptop isn't done yet — ChromeOS Flex is Google's free operating system that makes it fast again
posts.summary: ChromeOS Flex is Google's free operating system built for older computers, and it can help a slow old laptop feel quick again. It's free at chromeos.google/products/chromeos-flex — Google gives you the download and the steps to put it on a USB stick, and the laptop starts up from that stick. If that sounds like more than you want to tackle, that's exactly what I'm here for.
posts.truth: I see this all the time: a perfectly good 8- or 10-year-old laptop sitting in a drawer because 'it got slow' — and the owner is about to spend six hundred dollars on a new one. Most people don't realize the hardware is usually fine; the software on it just got too heavy. ChromeOS Flex strips it back to the basics — email, Facebook, banking, photos — and it doesn't bog down the way an old install does. It's not for everyone: if you depend on one specific Windows program, keep it. But for the customer who just wants email and pictures, I've seen a ten-year-old laptop feel faster after Flex than it did the day it was new.

posts.title: Is your flash drive crawling? Plug it into the blue USB port — it's many times faster and it's already on your computer
posts.summary: Look at the USB ports on your computer: some are black, some are blue. The blue ones are the fast kind — a flash drive or camera card reader can run many times quicker in them than in the old black ports. There's no software to download and nothing to install — just move the plug. If you don't have blue ports, the black ones still work fine; they're just slower.
posts.truth: I see this a few times a month: somebody says their flash drive is 'broken' or 'dying,' and it turns out it's been plugged into a slow port the whole time. A file that takes five minutes on the wrong port takes under a minute on the right one. Before you toss a drive or buy a new computer because things feel slow, try the blue port — it's the cheapest speed upgrade there is.

posts.title: Copy text out of any screenshot — the Windows Snipping Tool's Text Actions does it in one click
posts.summary: The Snipping Tool that's already on your Windows 11 computer can pull the words out of any screenshot. Press the Windows key + Shift + S to take a snip, click the Text Actions button at the top of the picture, then click Copy — now the words paste like normal text. Built into Windows, free, no download.
posts.truth: I used to watch customers retype an error message word for word off the screen because they didn't know their computer can read text out of pictures. The first time you drag a box around a screenshot and get real, copyable words, it feels like a magic trick — then you use it every single week.
